content: My honest opinion: I would have voted yes. Not because the life-expectancy link feels comfortable—it doesn’t—but because I think it is the less bad version of the truth. At 45, it can feel personal, like the system is quietly moving the line you had planned around. Especially in a place like Basel, where there are office jobs but also hospitals, logistics, crafts and physically demanding work, the risk is real that a higher age doesn’t land equally on everyone. That’s why I would have wanted strong safeguards for health, demanding jobs and part-time careers. Still, I think the AHV cannot keep acting as if a 20th-century lifespan still fits a 21st-century life. If we freeze the age while people live longer, the pressure will return as pension reductions, higher contributions or weaker finances for younger generations. The life-expectancy mechanism is unattractive because it is a ratchet, but I would rather have a system that adjusts honestly than one that quietly runs into trouble. So yes, with that caveat: yes to the direction, but only if it is not applied as a blunt rule to everyone.
